doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Origin of the idea for a jazz archive
summary: The idea grew from Gibson parties where musicians died, and a Joe Williams and Milt Hinton conversation he wished was taped.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Well you have a beautiful building named after you and I think the most lasting thing of course is going to be this jazz archive. And I’d love to just actually hear again how this idea came to your head.

Well it started with the Gibson parties in Colorado Springs and later in Denver, when I realized that every year some people did not appear again, they were gone. And they used to pay tribute to them. And I though jeez, there they’ve gone, and there’s nothing. There’s really nothing left behind. And then — I forget when it was — but it was Joe Williams and Milt Hinton were sitting down at the Alexander Hamilton Inn across the table. Joe was on one side and I was on the other and they started talking. And they went on with these anecdotes and so on. I said to Joe jeez, we ought to be taping that. Well I had previous to that tried like hell to get Dick Gibson to do something. I said we have to do something to preserve jazz. We have to. And he had a couple of ideas. I said okay, I’ll fund it. So I got in $50,000 I think it was, for matching, to match, and then we’d go ahead. We were going to do some things — not like the archives but sort of like it. And he just never got off his duff. Dick Gibson did a lot for jazz but basically he was a bum. And he just never did anything. And so we canceled that. And I’ve been querying people, what can we do preserve this? And Dave Berger, you know David Berger. David Berger is Milt Hinton’s Jewish son-in-law. His white, Jewish son. And Dave Berger called me © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
